messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mai was 35, married, and working as a physical therapist when she came for help, but the story she told began years earlier, in a relationship that she now described with visible strain and long pauses. She had been living in the United States since childhood, and the shame she carried seemed to sit beside the facts of the abuse as something she had never been able to put down. The relationship had begun in the usual way, with closeness and the ordinary trust of a romantic partner, but over time her former boyfriend became physically abusive. What she returned to most often was not a single dramatic injury but the feeling of being overpowered: being held, moved, and forced when she did not want to be. In her telling, the most lasting moments were the ones in which another person’s hands took control of her body and she had no way to stop it.

Even now, specific sensations could pull her back without warning. A particular temperature on the skin was enough to do it, especially when something cold or unexpectedly warm touched her body. At work, when she was demonstrating exercises or placing her hands on a patient’s shoulder, she sometimes became acutely aware of the temperature of skin against skin and would tense before she could stop herself. She also became unsettled by physical touch itself in ways that were difficult for her to explain in the moment. Even in ordinary professional contact, the brief pressure of a hand or the feel of another person’s grip could leave her abruptly guarded, as if she were bracing for something she could not name aloud. She had also become highly alert to people she read as potentially dangerous. In waiting rooms, parking lots, and crowded public places, her attention went immediately to posture, tone, and proximity, and she found herself scanning for people who might force their way in or ignore her boundaries. Being forced to do something remained especially potent. When anyone pressed her to agree quickly, or when she felt cornered into compliance, she would shut down internally and become preoccupied with how to escape without escalating the situation.

Her memories of the abuse did not stay in the past in any straightforward way. When a memory returned, it felt to Mai as if it were happening now rather than something finished long ago, with the same bodily alarm and the same sense of being trapped inside the moment. She described trying to tell her husband about parts of what had happened and finding that she could not keep the story together; she would lose the thread, stop mid-sentence, and feel embarrassed and flooded by feeling before she could finish. At times she had to stop entirely because the recall became so overwhelming that she could not push through it. She spoke about this with frustration, saying that she knew what had happened but could not get it out in a clean line. The memory arrived in fragments of force, skin, and fear, and each fragment seemed to carry the whole scene with it.

Alongside that, Mai spent a great deal of time dwelling on how she used to be before the abuse. She mourned the version of herself she remembered as more open, more relaxed, and less afraid of other people’s intentions. She also found herself repeatedly going over how the event could have been prevented, replaying decisions and conversations in an effort to identify the point at which things might have turned out differently. This kind of thinking often surfaced after work, when she was alone in the car or sitting at home after dinner, and it left her exhausted and discouraged. She was sure, in a way that had hardened over time, that the abuse happened because of the way she acted. Even though she could describe the relationship as abusive, she still returned to moments in which she wondered whether she had somehow invited it, tolerated too much, or failed to leave in time. From there it was only a short step to the belief that something was wrong with her as a person. She spoke about feeling permanently humiliated by what had happened, as though the abuse had marked her in a way others could somehow see.

Despite building a stable life and a professional identity that required calm, skill, and careful physical contact, Mai found that her daily routines were now arranged around vigilance. She worked hard to keep herself composed in the clinic, but certain patient interactions left her tense and scanning, especially when someone’s hands came into contact with hers or when she felt she was being pushed to proceed in a way she had not chosen. Over time, she noticed that the consequences reached beyond her own discomfort; she was less able to relax with her husband and more likely to withdraw after work, and she feared that people who cared about her might not understand why ordinary touch sometimes felt so loaded. She finally sought help because she was tired of living as if the abuse were still happening in the present. What brought her in was not only the severity of the symptoms, but the fear that she would remain trapped in humiliation, self-blame, and constant alertness forever. More than anything, Mai said she wanted to stop feeling as though her body and her life were still under someone else’s control.
